c.tagline: Cyprus's mosaic-rich harbour town where legend says Aphrodite rose from the sea.

taxi.fareNote: Urban taxis are metered; rural and intercity taxis use fixed zonal tariffs. Bolt coverage is limited, so most rides are booked by phone or picked up at ranks.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number; 199 also reaches police, ambulance, and fire in Cyprus.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Expect inflated drink prices and occasional bar scams along the Kato Paphos Bar Street nightlife strip.

hood_desc: The lower seafront town around the harbour, castle and the UNESCO-listed archaeological park with its Roman mosaics; the tourist heart, packed with hotels, tavernas and sights.
The upper old town (also called Ktima), built up the hillside around the covered market, Kennedy Square and the municipal gardens; more local, with shops, bakeries and everyday life.
The hotel strip running north from the harbour past the Tombs of the Kings, lined with resorts, beach bars and restaurants; convenient and lively, close to the sea.
A resort area about 12 km north near Peyia, built around a sheltered sandy bay and the gateway to the wild Akamas peninsula; relaxed and family-friendly.
A traditional village just east of Kato Paphos, known for its five-domed Agia Paraskevi church and Cyprus delight sweets; quieter and residential with easy beach access.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: OSYPA buses run roughly 6:00 AM to about 8:00-11:00 PM depending on the route, with reduced service in winter.
transit.note: Paphos has no rail or metro; the OSYPA bus network links Kato Paphos, the upper town (Ktima), Coral Bay and the airport. Service thins in the evenings and in winter, so taxis fill the gaps.
transit.pay: Bus fares are paid in cash to the driver (around €1.50 single, €5 day ticket, more at night). There is no contactless smartcard system as of 2026.

bus: OSYPA Paphos city and district buses
Intercity buses to Limassol and Nicosia

transit.m: Airport bus (route 612/613) to Kato Paphos and Karavella station (~30-40 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants if a service charge is not already included; rounding up for taxis and cafes is appreciated.

food.name: Kleftiko
food.desc: Lamb shoulder sealed in a clay oven for hours with garlic, lemon and bay until it falls off the bone. Cyprus at its most patient.

places.name: Viva Cyprus
places.note: Long-running taverna near the harbour repeatedly singled out by reviewers for its kleftiko.

places.name: Seven St Georges Tavern
places.note: Cult meze house cooking with foraged herbs and its own garden produce.

places.name: Yiannis Tavern
places.note: Hill-village taverna where kleftiko and sheftalia come as part of the house meze.

food.name: Souvla
food.desc: Fist-sized chunks of pork or lamb turned slowly on a long skewer over charcoal, served with lemon, pita and pickled cabbage.

places.name: Pagkratios Tavern
places.note: Neighbourhood grill in the old town praised for charcoal meats and village sausage.

places.name: Kings of Aphrodite
places.note: Traditional Cypriot tavern built around the charcoal grill and live bouzouki nights.

places.name: Laona Restaurant
places.note: Family-run lunch spot serving whatever is on the day list, souvla included.

food.name: Halloumi
food.desc: Cypriot mint-folded sheep and goat cheese, grilled until it squeaks and blisters. Eaten hot with watermelon or lountza ham.

places.name: Pagkratios Tavern
places.note: Serves village halloumi grilled to order alongside the meze parade.

places.name: Seven St Georges Tavern
places.note: Uses small-batch local cheese; halloumi appears in several meze plates.

places.name: Paphos Municipal Market
places.note: Buy fresh and aged halloumi straight from village producers in the covered agora.

food.name: Fish meze
food.desc: A rolling twenty-plate procession of dips, octopus, calamari, prawns and grilled catch. Order it hungry and clear the evening.

places.name: Ttakkas Bay Tavern
places.note: Seaside taverna known for very fresh fish and generous meze portions.

places.name: Seven St Georges Tavern
places.note: Its meze runs to dozens of dishes and changes with the season.

places.name: Ouzeri Paphos Harbour
places.note: Harbourfront ouzeri pairing small fish plates with ouzo and zivania.

food.name: Sheftalia
food.desc: Coarse pork and onion mince wrapped in caul fat and grilled, so the wrapping melts and bastes the meat. The island best sausage.

places.name: Yiannis Tavern
places.note: Village kitchen where sheftalia are made in-house and grilled over wood.

places.name: Ettas Tavern
places.note: Longstanding local favourite for straightforward grilled Cypriot classics.

places.name: Kings of Aphrodite
places.note: Charcoal grill turning out sheftalia, souvla and loukanika nightly.

food.name: Loukoumades
food.desc: Yeasted dough balls fried to order, drowned in carob syrup or honey and dusted with cinnamon. The standard Cypriot end to a meal.

places.name: Seven St Georges Tavern
places.note: Finishes its meze with hot loukoumades and homemade preserves.

places.name: Zorbas Bakery
places.note: Cyprus bakery chain selling loukoumades, daktyla and other syrup sweets all day.

places.name: Paphos Municipal Market
places.note: Stalls around the market fry loukoumades and sell Geroskipou loukoumi.

food.name: Zivania
food.desc: Clear grape-pomace spirit distilled in Cyprus since Venetian times, 45 percent and up. Served ice cold in thimble glasses with meze.

places.name: Ouzeri Paphos Harbour
places.note: Harbour bar pouring zivania and ouzo with small plates, the way locals drink it.

places.name: Vasilikon Winery
places.note: Paphos-district winery on the wine route with tastings of local wines and spirits.

places.name: Kings of Aphrodite
places.note: Traditional tavern where a zivania round usually arrives with the bill.

food.name: Commandaria
food.desc: Sun-dried sweet wine from the Troodos foothills, claimed as the world oldest named wine. Amber, raisiny, sipped after dinner.

places.name: Sterna Winery

landmarks: Kato Paphos Archaeological Park
A UNESCO World Heritage site by the harbor, where the Houses of Dionysos and Theseus preserve some of the Mediterranean's most exquisite Roman floor mosaics.
Tombs of the Kings
A hauntingly grand necropolis of the Hellenistic era, its subterranean burial chambers carved with Doric columns straight from the seaside bedrock.
Paphos Castle & Harbour
A stout medieval fort guarding the palm-lined harbor promenade, backdrop to the September Aphrodite opera festival and countless sunset strolls.
Petra tou Romiou (Aphrodite's Rock)
The mythic sea stack where the goddess of love rose from the foam, framed by a pebble beach and impossibly blue swirling water.
St Paul's Pillar & Ayia Kyriaki Church
Amid early-Christian basilica ruins stands the pillar where tradition says the apostle Paul was flogged before converting Cyprus's Roman governor.
Agios Neophytos Monastery
A hillside monastery founded by a hermit in 1159, whose cave hermitage, the Enkleistra, glows with remarkable Byzantine frescoes.
Coral Bay
Paphos's favorite beach escape, a sheltered crescent of golden sand between limestone headlands with calm, family-friendly turquoise water.
Akamas Peninsula & Blue Lagoon
A wild protected peninsula of gorges, juniper and sea-turtle beaches, whose dazzling Blue Lagoon is the day-cruise highlight from nearby Latchi.
Ktima (Paphos Old Town)
The upper town's regenerated historic core, where a restored municipal market, Ottoman baths and vivid street art repay an unhurried wander.
Sea Caves at Peyia
A sculpted stretch of white chalk cliffs and wave-carved arches near Coral Bay, a photographer's magnet at golden hour.

train.note: Cyprus has no railway at all. The Cyprus Government Railway ran its last train on 31 December 1951 and the track was lifted by 1953, while the final narrow-gauge mining lines closed in 1974; only the museum at Evrychou station remains. Proposals to reinstate a line resurface periodically but nothing is under construction, so every land journey on the island is by bus, taxi or hire car.

bus.note: Intercity Buses (https://www.intercity-buses.com/) links Paphos with Limassol in about an hour, Nicosia in roughly two, and onward to Larnaca and Ayia Napa, using stops at the Karavella station in Ktima and near the harbour in Kato Paphos. Local and district services, including the routes to Coral Bay, Polis and Latchi and the shuttles to Paphos Airport, are run by OSYPA (https://www.pafosbuses.com/), with fares paid to the driver or on the Motion smartcard. There are no international coaches from the Republic of Cyprus because the island's only land boundary is the UN buffer zone, crossed at designated checkpoints rather than by through bus.

ferry.note: Paphos harbour is a small craft and fishing port: what leaves from it are day-cruise catamarans and glass-bottom boats up the coast to Coral Bay, Lara and the Akamas Blue Lagoon, plus tenders from the occasional cruise ship anchored offshore. There is no scheduled ferry, and the Republic of Cyprus has had no regular international passenger sailing since the seasonal Limassol-Piraeus trial ended - Limassol, about 70 km and an hour east, is where any such service would resume. The nearest working international crossing is Kyrenia to Tasucu in Turkey from the north of the island, run by Akgunler (https://www.akgunlerbilet.com/) in about 2.5 hours.

half.name: Troodos Mountains
half.blurb: Pine-forested peaks with Byzantine painted churches and mountain villages lie about an hour from Paphos.

half.name: Limassol
half.blurb: Cyprus's second city has a medieval castle and an old-town marina, roughly an hour east of Paphos.

half.name: Polis and Latchi
half.blurb: A quiet coastal town near the Akamas Peninsula's fig-tree bay sits about forty-five minutes north of Paphos.

half.name: Omodos
half.blurb: A wine village with a monastery and a cobblestone square in the Troodos foothills is about an hour away.
